source.title: On Generalization of Adaptive Methods for Over-parameterized Linear Regression
source.authors: Vatsal Shah; S. Basu; Anastasios Kyrillidis; S. Sanghavi

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some table references and mathematical symbols appear corrupted or flattened, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: It compares adaptive and non-adaptive training methods on held-out performance, addressing optimizer-dependent generalization with experiments and measures different from the cited optimizer study. It does not test random-label memorization or the other claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own comparisons of held-out accuracy for adaptive and non-adaptive methods on image classifiers. Results cited from prior work and linear-regression experiments are not used as rows for V4. Figure-based comparisons have no recoverable numerical values; the paper describes their direction in text.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares held-out image-classification accuracy of adaptive optimizers and SGD variants after tuning step size, momentum, and decay schedules. These experiments test V4; the linear-regression theory and synthetic experiments fall outside its benchmark scope.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the empirical conclusion: adaptive methods can generalize as well as non-adaptive methods, relative performance depends on the problem and data, and both require tuning. The paper's central theoretical conclusion concerns how preconditioner structure and initialization determine convergence in over-parameterized linear regression.
record.recipe_differences: Compares adaptive methods including Adam, AdaGrad, and RMSProp with SGD variants on held-out accuracy, rather than replicating the specific benchmark protocol of Wilson et al. Hyperparameters were tuned over stated step-size, momentum, and decay choices.
record.method_sensitivity: The relative performance varied by architecture and parameterization. The authors report that optimizer step size, momentum, and decay choices matter, and that results depend on problem/data; batch sizes were kept identical.

fits_no_version.finding: Synthetic linear-regression experiments and theory show that adaptive preconditioners can produce equal, better, or worse generalization than gradient descent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer-dependent generalization in over-parameterized linear regression depends on data, initialization, and preconditioner structure.

fits_no_version.finding: Adam matches or exceeds SGD accuracy on MobileNet architectures despite approximately twice the Euclidean weight norm.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Euclidean weight norm alone does not consistently order image-classifier generalization across optimizers.

record.problems: The deep-learning comparisons rely substantially on plots whose numerical values are not provided in the text. The authors note that more comprehensive reasoning would require multiple runs per network because initialization and other hyperparameters may affect differences. Hyperparameter tuning was limited to tested step-size and momentum sets, with default values for remaining parameters.
record.rows_left_out: No additional held-out optimizer comparison rows were recoverable as separate model-specific outcomes beyond those listed. Synthetic linear-regression results and cited results were excluded because V4 specifies image-classification and language benchmarks.

untested.parts: No comparison of random-label memorization with natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy.
No width sweep beyond a demonstrated zero-training-error threshold; under- versus over-parameterized architectures do not establish the claimed width trend.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.

No language benchmarks, broader tuning intervention, decoupled weight decay, or optimizer switching; the supplied prose does not establish equal or better adaptive training performance for each accuracy comparison.
No batch-size intervention; batch sizes are held identical.
No magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness or ranking of generalization gaps.
No removal and retraining experiment involving memorized examples.

missing.what: Separate C1 AdaGrad and AdaGrad-variant accuracy comparisons. The text reports underperformance, which the Adam/RMSProp-focused R7 and R8 omit; verify the allocation across C1-UP and C1-OP from the figure.
missing.locator: Appendix B.3, CIFAR10 dataset and C1 architecture, page 20; B.3.2, page 21; Figure 4

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for V4. Accuracy comparisons are qualitative; no numerical plot values were reconstructed. Tuning includes momentum as well as learning rate and decay, so the protocol differs somewhat from V4's narrow tuning condition. Architecture-specific challenges do not establish that adaptive methods never generalize worse.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out performance are not compared.
No network-width sweep around the interpolation threshold.
No language benchmarks; no broad hyperparameter search beyond step size, momentum, and decay choices; no test of decoupled weight decay or switching optimizers.
Batch size is held identical across experiments, not varied.
Dropout is part of some architectures but is not varied as an intervention.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or generalization-gap ranking comparison.
No removal of memorized training examples.

rows.subject: PreActResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Compared plain gradient descent with adaptive methods on CIFAR-100; the paper reports the plain-gradient models had slightly better performance.

conditions.value: plain gradient descent versus adaptive methods

rows.note: The text calls the plain-gradient performance slightly better; it does not provide numerical accuracy values.
rows.check: The text reports only a slight advantage for non-adaptive methods. The direction is readable from the prose despite unavailable numerical plot values.

rows.subject: MobileNet
rows.operation_detail: Compared Adam with plain gradient methods on CIFAR-100; Adam had at least as good generalization.
rows.locator: Figure 3, left middle panel; Section 3.2; Appendix B.3
rows.note: The paper states Adam had at least as good generalization and 2× larger l2-norm weights; precise accuracy values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Adam generalizes at least as well as non-adaptive methods, so the claimed adaptive-optimizer penalty is absent. The text does not distinguish equality from an advantage.

rows.subject: M1-UP shallow CNN + FFN experiments (10 Monte-Carlo realizations)
rows.operation_detail: Compared adaptive methods with simple SGD variants on MNIST; Adam and RMSProp performed similarly to SGD variants, while AdaGrad and its variant performed worse.
rows.baseline: simple SGD variants; numerical baseline not stated
rows.value: Adam and RMSProp performed similarly; AdaGrad and its variant did not perform as well as the rest
rows.uncertainty: standard deviations plotted for M1 experiments; numerical values not stated
rows.locator: Figure 4; Appendix B.3, MNIST dataset and M1 architecture; B.3.2 Results
rows.note: Qualitative result described in the text; the plotted accuracy values are not stated numerically.
rows.check: Split by optimizer: AdaGrad and its variant underperform, making the penalty observed; Adam and RMSProp match SGD variants, making it absent. One state cannot represent both results. The relevant architecture-specific discussion is in Appendix B.3, page 20.

rows.subject: M1-OP shallow CNN + FFN experiments (10 Monte-Carlo realizations)
rows.operation_detail: Compared adaptive methods with SGD on MNIST; all adaptive methods performed similarly to SGD.
rows.value: adaptive methods performed similarly to SGD
rows.uncertainty: standard deviations plotted for M1 experiments; numerical values not stated
rows.locator: Figure 4; Appendix B.3, MNIST dataset and M1 architecture; B.3.2 Results
rows.note: The text also says SGD momentum performed less favorably than plain SGD, conjecturing non-optimal tuning.
rows.check: All adaptive methods perform similarly to plain SGD. Momentum SGD performs worse than plain SGD and must remain a separate comparator condition.

rows.subject: C1-UP shallow CNN + FFN experiments (10 Monte-Carlo realizations)
rows.operation_detail: Compared adaptive methods with simple SGD variants on CIFAR-10; Adam and RMSProp performed better than their non-adaptive counterparts in the described C1 experiments.
rows.baseline: non-adaptive counterparts; numerical baseline not stated
rows.value: Adam and RMSProp achieved the best performance
rows.uncertainty: standard deviations plotted; numerical values not stated
rows.locator: Figure 4; Appendix B.3, CIFAR10 dataset and C1 architecture; B.3.2 Results
rows.note: The prose describes Adam and RMSProp as achieving the best performance for both under- and over-parameterized C1 settings.
rows.check: Adam/RMSProp show no adaptive penalty. Appendix B.3 first describes them as best, then as similar to SGD, so reversal versus equality is unresolved. Specify Adam/RMSProp as the subjects; AdaGrad has a different outcome. C1-UP uses 350 epochs.
